narration: The Midnight Circle: The Living Ritual of the Mitote.
This is Mitote. Pre-Hispanic to present.
on_screen: Title card: Mitote · Mexico · Pre-Hispanic to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance emerged shortly after the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire, based on the old 'mitote' dance.
It was adapted to include Catholic symbolism to preserve ancient rituals.
Its origins are ascribed to the Bajío region, Querétaro, and Tlaxcala.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is performed for spiritual and personal reasons, often starting at midnight to call upon ancestors.
It is linked to religious festivals such as the Santa Cruz in Chalma, Santiago Apóstol, and the Virgin of Guadalupe.
It serves as a ritual cleansing and a way to honor family and cultural ancestors.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers organize into circles, often with an inner circle of elders and an outer circle of younger dancers.
The circle is divided into four sections marking the cardinal directions.
Movement is restricted to the feet and torso, leaving hands free for instruments and rattles.
Watch for Cardinal marking.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Circular formation divided into four sections corresponding to cardinal directions.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is driven by pre-Hispanic instruments including the huehuetl (drum), teponaztli (drum), and conch shell trumpets.
The 'concha' (a lute made from an armadillo shell) represents Spanish influence.
Listen for the huehuetl, teponaztli, conch shell trumpets, conchas (lute).

A percussive, earthy sound dominated by the deep resonance of huehuetl and teponaztli drums, layered with the sharp, rhythmic rattling of ayoyotes and the melodic, stringed quality of the concha lute.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Regalia ranges from tunics (naguillas) and capes with gold and silver adornments to loincloths and natural materials for 'Azteca' dancers.
Headdresses are made of ostrich or pheasant feathers.
The setting is often a church atrium or a public square, decorated with altars, flowers, candles, and incense smoke.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Andres Segura, Florencio Yescas, Jesús González, La Nanita, Jefe Sonora, Jefe Ortíz, Jefe Aranda.
The 'Apaches' style in San Luis Potosí, which uses trousers, brightly colored shirts, and wooden bows.
The tradition is passed down through 'mesas' (tables) that trace their lineage to a 'dance forefather' named in the group's standard.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: The dance is a ritual ceremony involving ancestor worship and spiritual cleansing; outsiders should respect the sacred space and not solicit donations or interfere with the ritual.
